mem.t: And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men, knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.

lessons.title: God, the First Worker
lessons.theme: Work was not invented by us; God himself showed us how

v: The heavens, the earth, and all their vast array were finished.
On the seventh day God finished his work which he had done; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had done.
God blessed the seventh day, and made it holy, because he rested in it from all his work of creation which he had done.
But Jesus answered them, “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.”

lessons.still: Before you start work, pause for thirty seconds. Breathe deeply and say, “Lord, you were the first to work. I am not going to work alone today; I am working alongside you.” Place your to-do list in his hands.
teach: Open the Bible at page one, and the first worker on the scene is not Adam but God. Over six days he separates light from darkness, sets the boundaries of sea and land, plants the grass and arranges the stars. He designs, builds and inspects the quality, and at the end he sees that everything he has made is very good. Work is not a chore humanity invented after the fall; it is the pattern of God himself.

So when you switch on your computer, walk onto a building site, step up to a classroom whiteboard or pick up a customer-service call, you are doing something God-like: bringing order out of chaos and creating value where there was nothing. Like an apprentice watching a master craftsman, our work imitates the great Engineer of heaven.

When God finished his work, he rested and blessed the seventh day. He did not rest because he was tired, but to enjoy, celebrate and delight in what he had made. Jesus said, “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.” Today he is still at work in your workplace. You are not working for God as a hired hand; you are working with God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example — the Father works, and the Son works. Change your thinking and your life changes: from ‘I am slaving for my boss’ to ‘I am working with God’. The focus is not the payslip but the Lord who works beside me.
lessons.scene: Zhiming is a warehouse keeper at a logistics company. Every day he counts stock, shelves goods and reconciles inventory. He often wonders, ‘What does this kind of work have to do with God?’ Then one day he realises that the shelves he carefully arranged have saved the whole team two hours of overtime.
q: Who is God? — From the six days of creation, what kind of worker do you see God to be?
Who am I? — Do you usually see your job as a chore, a way to pay the bills, or working alongside God?
How shall I respond? — Which task today could you complete with a God-like attitude?
lessons.jesus: The people of Nazareth called Jesus ‘the carpenter’ (Mark 6:3). He shaped timber, made tools and was paid wages. Long before he began to preach, his hands were rough from the workbench. The hands nailed to the cross were also the hands of a working man.
lessons.pray: Lord, Creator of heaven and earth, thank you for showing me the dignity of work. Work with me today; let what my hands do be good, and let my heart be set not merely on my salary but on you. I give you every task of this day. Be King in my work. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: First thing at work, pray: ‘Lord, today I work with you’
Pick one routine task and do it to a ‘very good’ standard
Before leaving, spend one minute thanking God for today’s work
lessons.noon: “My Father is still working, so I am working, too.” — Lord, right now I lay down my restlessness and keep working in your presence.

lessons.title: The Caretaker of the Garden
lessons.theme: God placed the world in our hands to cultivate and keep it

v: The LORD God planted a garden eastward, in Eden, and there he put the man whom he had formed.

Out of the ground the LORD God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
The LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.

lessons.still: Before you open your laptop, lay both hands open on the desk and say, “Lord, this desk and this job are a garden you have entrusted to me. Today I am here to cultivate and keep it, not to claim it as my own.” Then begin your first task.
teach: “The LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Notice that before there was any sin, God gave the man work. Eden was not a holiday resort; it was a garden waiting to be tended. To cultivate carries the sense of tilling and serving; to keep means to guard and watch over. God planted the garden first, then placed the man in it. From the very beginning, work was a trust from God, not a human invention.

Imagine you have just taken over as building manager of a large block of flats. On day one your predecessor hands you a heavy bunch of keys: the plant room, the roof, the underground car park. You are not the owner, yet you are responsible for every door. Leaks must be fixed, strangers questioned, residents cared for. Work is like that. Reports, clients, teams and machines are keys placed in your hand. A caretaker’s honour lies not in owning but in being faithful.

The self-centred life treats a trust as territory: ‘my department, my clients, my credit.’ We guard it tightly yet tend it poorly. To let Jesus be King is to admit that he owns the garden and I am simply the one placed in it. Once that thought changes, life loosens its grip. I no longer need to fear for my position; I simply cultivate and keep where I have been placed today, and one day give my account to the Lord.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is laying down power and returning to our proper place. Our place is gardener, not owner — letting people be people and God be God. When I return to being ‘the one placed here’, work stops being a battlefield to prove myself and becomes a garden in which I serve God.
lessons.scene: Ah De is the caretaker of an ageing housing estate in Taichung. At a residents’ meeting, someone publicly blames him for the mess in the recycling area. Afterwards the committee chair says quietly, ‘Just push it onto the cleaning company — you didn’t sign their contract.’ Ah De holds the collection schedule, wondering whether to do an extra round of the bin room himself each night.
q: Who is God? — God planted the garden first and then placed the man in it. What kind of master is he?
Who am I? — Are you more of a territory-guarder, or a steward who cultivates and keeps?
How shall I respond? — If you were Ah De, how would ‘cultivate and keep’ shape what you do with that collection schedule?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep” (John 10:11). A hired hand runs when the wolf comes; he stands in front of the flock, even to the point of death. He is the most faithful keeper of all, and keeps us to the end. Because of him, we too can learn to keep others gladly.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for placing me in this role. I confess that this is not my territory but your garden. Give me diligence to cultivate and alertness to keep, so that I treat every colleague, every file and every customer in my care with kindness. When I want to pass the buck or grab the credit, remind me that you are the owner. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: List three ‘keys’ in your hands today and pray over each
Fix one small thing you have long put off
Before you leave, check what needs keeping for the next shift
lessons.noon: “The LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.” — Lord, right now I return to the place you put me, and keep it faithfully.

lessons.title: Wearing His Image to Work
lessons.theme: Made in God’s image, our work is glorious stewardship, not a curse

v: God said, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
God created man in his own image. In God’s image he created him; male and female he created them.

God blessed them. God said to them, “Be fruitful, multiply, fill the earth, and subdue it. Have dominion over the fish of the sea, over the birds of the sky, and over every living thing that moves on the earth.”
what is man, that you think of him? What is the son of man, that you care for him?
For you have made him a little lower than the angels, and crowned him with glory and honour.
You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:

lessons.still: As you glance in the mirror before leaving, pause for thirty seconds and say, “Lord, I bear your image. When people see my work today, may they catch a glimpse of you.” Straighten your collar and carry that dignity out of the door.
teach: At the summit of creation God says, “Let’s make man in our image, after our likeness. Let them have dominion…” (Genesis 1:26). Image and dominion belong together: because we are made like God, we are entrusted with caring for the earth. Work existed before the fall. It is not God’s punishment on humanity but his crown for us. The psalmist says God has “crowned him with glory and honour” and made him “ruler over the works of your hands” (Psalm 8:5–6).

In the ancient world, kings set up statues of themselves throughout their territory to declare, ‘This land is mine.’ God placed his image on human beings and set them in the world: you are God’s image set up in your workplace. Think of a regional manager posted overseas by head office. She is not the owner, yet clients come to know the company through her. How you run a meeting, answer an email or handle a complaint speaks for that ‘head office’.

Dominion is not control but representation. Self-centred management wants to be king: ‘Do it my way.’ Image-bearing management wants to reflect the King: ‘Do it his way.’ Change your thinking and your life changes. When ‘I am just earning a living’ becomes ‘I am bearing God’s image at work’, the same meeting table becomes a place to show God’s character: fairness, creativity, faithfulness and mercy.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of perspective — from the human view that work is a curse to God’s view that work is a crown. Let Jesus receive all the glory: managing well does not prove how capable I am; it lets people see the God who made me.
lessons.scene: Yating has just been promoted to team leader at an advertising agency, managing four people more experienced than she is. Her very first pitch is rejected by the client. She badly wants to name, in the group chat, whose artwork caused the problem, to save face. The message is typed, and her finger hovers over ‘Send’.
q: Who is God? — Why does God entrust dominion to those made in his image?
Who am I? — Is your way of leading more like playing king, or reflecting the King?
How shall I respond? — If you were Yating, bearing God’s image, how would you rewrite that message?
lessons.jesus: Jesus “is the image of the invisible God” (Colossians 1:15). He reflected the Father perfectly: he rebuked the wind and waves, and he stooped to wash his disciples’ feet. In him we see that true authority is service, and in him our damaged image is being made new.
lessons.pray: God who made me, thank you for placing your image on me and giving me the crown of stewardship. Forgive me for so often treating authority as face and colleagues as tools. Today, in meetings and in messages, let me reflect your justice and gentleness, so that people see you through my work. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Think of one team member and affirm them specifically today
Before sending, reread: does this reflect God’s character?
Publicly credit the team for something you could claim
lessons.noon: “God created man in his own image.” — Lord, right now let my words and decisions reflect your likeness.

lessons.title: The Workbench at Nazareth
lessons.theme: Jesus worked through hidden years, making ordinary work holy

v: He went out from there. He came into his own country, and his disciples followed him.

When the Sabbath had come, he began to teach in the synagogue, and many hearing him were astonished, saying, “Where did this man get these things?” and, “What is the wisdom that is given to this man, that such mighty works come about by his hands?
Isn’t this the carpenter, the son of Mary and brother of James, Joses, Judah, and Simon? Aren’t his sisters here with us?” So they were offended at him.
And he went down with them and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them, and his mother kept all these sayings in her heart.
And Jesus increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and men.

lessons.still: On the train or on foot, touch your staff pass or your tools and pray, “Lord Jesus, you also worked day after day. Today I do these unseen things for you.” Then breathe quietly three times.
teach: The people of his home town asked, “Isn’t this the carpenter?” (Mark 6:3). The original word can describe a builder who worked in wood or stone. The Gospels are almost silent about Jesus’ life before thirty, telling us only that “he was subject to them” and “increased in wisdom and stature, and in favour with God and men” (Luke 2:51–52). We do not know how many doorframes or ploughs he made, but we can imagine that his work was ordinary and repetitive, so familiar to the neighbours that they later took offence at him.

When you use a good app, you see a beautiful screen but not the back end: servers, databases, lines of code that nobody ever praises. Yet if the back end fails, the whole system crashes. Jesus’ years in Nazareth were like the back end of the plan of salvation. Your unseen reconciliations, prep work, rosters and cleaning are back-end work for the kingdom of God too.

The self-centred heart dreads being overlooked: ‘I do so much — why does no one notice?’ Yet Jesus waited willingly at a small-town workbench for the Father’s appointed time. The self-emptied life does not mean disappearing; it means handing the matter of being seen over to God. God does not measure the size of the stage but the obedience of the heart. When you are faithful behind the scenes today, you are learning the likeness of Christ.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Jesus is my example — he obeyed in Nazareth before he preached in Galilee. Life first, then relationships, then ministry: the hidden years are not wasted; they are where a life is shaped.
lessons.scene: Guanyu has spent three years doing system maintenance at a tech company in Hsinchu. His peers have moved on to new products and conference stages. This week his manager asks him to take over an old system nobody wants to touch. After work Guanyu opens a job-search site, the cursor resting on ‘Submit CV’.
q: Who is God? — Why did God let his Son spend long, ordinary years in Nazareth?
Who am I? — When no one notices your work, what voice do you hear most in your heart?
How shall I respond? — Before deciding whether to apply elsewhere, how might Guanyu approach the work in front of him?
lessons.jesus: The Lord who holds all things together once worked in a small town, earned wages and was known to the neighbours as ‘the carpenter’. He felt no shame in ordinary work. This same Jesus, content to be hidden, later went to the cross for us, so that even our ordinary days are redeemed.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you worked quietly in Nazareth. Thank you for showing me that unseen work still has worth in your eyes. I confess that I crave being noticed and praised. Make me faithful behind the scenes and obedient as I wait. If I need to change direction, lead me clearly, and do not let me run away out of resentment. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Do one small thing nobody will notice, and offer it to the Lord
Thank one ‘back-end’ colleague: cleaner, admin or IT
Write down: ‘Which part of me is this job shaping?’
lessons.noon: “Isn’t this the carpenter?” — Lord, right now, in ordinary work, I want to obey as you did.

lessons.title: My Workplace Calling Statement
lessons.theme: Write down ‘working for the Lord’ as the compass for every workday

v: Whatever you do, in word or in deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks to God the Father through him.
And whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men,
knowing that from the Lord you will receive the reward of the inheritance; for you serve the Lord Christ.

lessons.still: Before work today, turn your phone face down for thirty seconds. Quietly say, “Lord, I am yours, and my work belongs to you.” Then type the first line in your notes app: ‘I am here in order to…’
teach: Paul was writing to servants in the church at Colossae. Most had no freedom to choose their work, yet Paul says, “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). He does not first change their jobs; he changes the ‘boss’ they see: “You serve the Lord Christ” (Colossians 3:24). This week we have seen that God is the first worker, that he placed us in the garden, gave us his image and dominion, and that his Son himself worked in Nazareth.

Every job comes with a job description listing your responsibilities and KPIs. But it only tells you what to do, not whom you do it for or why. A calling statement is a second job description for your life — not issued by your company, but written by God. It does not replace your task list, but it changes the heart with which you complete every task.

Today, write three or four sentences: ‘God is my true boss; I have been placed at ___; I want to be like Jesus by ___; through my work I want people to see ___.’ Changing your thinking begins with clear information. Ask the Holy Spirit for revelation until you are truly convinced and ready to put it into practice. Make it your phone wallpaper or stick it beside your screen, so that on Monday morning the first thing you see is your calling, not your anxiety.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The eight steps begin with information, revelation, conviction and practice. Ask the Spirit to turn this week’s information into revelation; writing your statement is a step into practice. The two cores: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.
lessons.scene: Joanne works in compliance at a bank in Singapore. Every day she catches errors, rejects files and writes reports, and the sales team often treat her as ‘the one in the way’. On Sunday evening she sits at her desk to write a calling statement but manages only one line: ‘I’m just doing a job.’ She stares at it, unsure whether to delete it or keep writing.
q: Who is God? — How does “you serve the Lord Christ” change your understanding of who your boss is?
Who am I? — If you had to describe your work identity in one sentence right now, what would you write?
How shall I respond? — If you were Joanne, how would you turn ‘I’m just doing a job’ into a calling statement?
lessons.jesus: Jesus said, “My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work” (John 4:34). His whole life had a clear calling: the Father sent him, and he completed the Father’s work until he cried from the cross, “It is finished!” When we write a calling statement, we are following the Lord who has already finished everything.
lessons.pray: Lord, you are my true boss. I am not just doing a job; I am serving you. Help me write down the calling you have given me, and help me live it every day: honest when misunderstood, wholehearted when the work is repetitive, and mindful under pressure that I am working for you. I place this statement and my Monday in your hands. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write your workplace calling statement in three or four lines
Make it your phone wallpaper or stick it by your screen
Send it to a spiritual companion and ask them to pray
lessons.noon: “You serve the Lord Christ.” — Lord, right now I remember that I am working for you.

mem.t: For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.

lessons.title: Come to Him, Then Go
lessons.theme: Calling begins with following Jesus; only then are we sent

v: Passing along by the sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and Andrew, the brother of Simon, casting a net into the sea, for they were fishermen.
Jesus said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men.”
Immediately they left their nets, and followed him.
He went up into the mountain and called to himself those whom he wanted, and they went to him.
He appointed twelve, that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach

lessons.still: Before you open your work chats, close your eyes for thirty seconds and say, “Lord Jesus, I come to you first. Every place I go and every person I meet today, I set out from you.” Then open the first message.
teach: Walking by the Sea of Galilee, Jesus saw Simon and Andrew casting a net and said to them, “Come after me, and I will make you into fishers for men” (Mark 1:17). The order of the call is clear: first ‘come after me’, then ‘fishers for men’. Later, on the mountain, Jesus appointed twelve, and Mark spells out why: “that they might be with him, and that he might send them out to preach” (Mark 3:14). Presence first, then sending; first to him, then out.

Every morning you charge your phone before you leave the house. Nobody decides that, because today is packed, they will skip the charging and just go — that only guarantees the phone dies when you need it most. Many Christian professionals understand calling only as ‘go’: go and hit targets, go and serve, go and make an impact. They forget that the source of calling is ‘come to me’. Without that charging cable, even the most zealous ‘going’ runs flat by three in the afternoon.

Self-centred service revolves around the task and uses busyness to prove its worth. The self-emptied life revolves around Jesus and bears fruit naturally from his presence. This is what 321 means by life first, then relationships, then ministry. Calling is not first of all a job but a person — Jesus. He calls you to follow him in the workplace, and first he asks you to be with him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The order of relationships is God, self, others, tasks. Calling starts with ‘come to me’: when our relationship with God comes first, our work has roots. Rely on the heart and the Spirit, not on the head and the self — be with him first, then set out.
lessons.scene: Jianguo runs a fifty-person metalworking factory in Dongguan and is on the shop floor by six every morning to check shipments. He is a deacon and likes to say, ‘My work is my ministry.’ Early this morning he opens a Bible he has not read for weeks, and his phone rings: a major client wants today’s delivery brought forward. He looks at the phone, then at the open page.
q: Who is God? — Why did Jesus want his disciples to be with him before he sent them out?
Who am I? — Does your sense of calling lean towards ‘go’, or does it also include ‘come to him’?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jianguo, how would you protect time with the Lord before and after that call?
lessons.jesus: Jesus lived this way himself. After a draining day of healing crowds, “early in the morning, while it was still dark, he rose up” and went to a deserted place to pray (Mark 1:35). He came out from the Father and returned to the Father. He calls us to follow not only his work but his intimate life with the Father.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, you called me first to come after you. Thank you for wanting me to be with you. I confess that I often mistake busyness for faithfulness and targets for calling. Before every call and every order today, draw me back to your side. Let me set out from your presence and carry your peace to my clients and colleagues. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Read one verse before opening work messages
Set a midday alarm and spend one minute with the Lord
On the way home, tell the Lord about today’s hardest moment
lessons.noon: “Come after me” — Lord, right now I come back to your side before I carry on.

lessons.title: Bezalel’s Workshop
lessons.theme: The Spirit fills not only the pulpit but the workshop

v: The LORD spoke to Moses, saying,
“Behold, I have called by name Bezalel the son of Uri, the son of Hur, of the tribe of Judah.
I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship,
to devise skilful works, to work in gold, and in silver, and in bronze,
and in cutting of stones for setting, and in carving of wood, to work in all kinds of workmanship.

lessons.still: As you wash your hands or pull on your work gloves, do it slowly and say, “Holy Spirit, fill these hands today. What I make is not only work; it is an offering to you.” Then pick up your first tool.
teach: The first person in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God is not a prophet or a priest but a craftsman. God says, “I have called by name Bezalel… I have filled him with the Spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all kinds of workmanship” (Exodus 31:2–3). Gold, silver, bronze, gemstones, timber — Bezalel’s calling was craftsmanship, and his craft was for building God’s tabernacle.

In a fine restaurant, the head chef checks every plate before it leaves the pass: the curve of the sauce, the temperature, the placement on the plate. Whether a dish is good depends not only on the ingredients but on the heart behind the hands. When God called Bezalel by name, it was like a chef singling out an apprentice: ‘This dish is yours.’ Your report, your code, the air conditioner you repaired — each can be craftsmanship the Spirit has called by name.

We often assume the Holy Spirit works only in Sunday songs and prayers, leaving us to our own devices from Monday to Friday. Bezalel tells us that God’s Spirit fills the workshop too. Rely on the heart and the Spirit, not on the head and the self — not abandoning expertise, but looking to his wisdom within it. When your craft is done for God’s glory, you are building God’s order in the workplace.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The Holy Spirit is my guide. Bezalel’s wisdom and skill came from God’s Spirit. Letting Jesus receive all the glory means signing every piece of work with his name instead of mine.
lessons.scene: Peishan runs a small patisserie studio in Kuala Lumpur. An influencer orders fifty gift boxes and wants the packaging to say ‘100% handmade, fully organic’, though two of the ingredients are not organic. ‘Everyone writes that,’ the client says. ‘Nobody checks.’ Peishan holds the printed label proofs and has not yet replied.
q: Who is God? — God called Bezalel by name and filled him with his Spirit. What does this tell you about him?
Who am I? — Do you believe the Spirit wants to fill your professional skills and craft?
How shall I respond? — If you were Peishan, how would Spirit-filled craftsmanship shape what you do with those labels?
lessons.jesus: Bezalel built the tabernacle so that God could dwell among his people; Jesus is the true tabernacle. “The Word became flesh and lived amongst us” (John 1:14) — the word for ‘lived’ means to pitch a tent. Bezalel’s craft points to a greater Builder, who in his own body opened the meeting place between God and us.
lessons.pray: Holy Spirit, thank you for filling not only the pulpit but the workshop. Give me wisdom, understanding, knowledge and every kind of skill, so that my work is honest, excellent and beautiful. When others want me to exaggerate or cut corners, give me courage to say no. May the real signature on my work be the name of the Lord Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Check the quality once more before today’s work goes out
Refuse one exaggerated or misleading marketing claim
Thank God for one of your professional skills
lessons.noon: “I have filled him with the Spirit of God” — Lord, right now fill my hands and my heart.

lessons.title: Your Name Is on the Table
lessons.theme: We are God’s workmanship, created for good works he prepared

v: for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God,
not of works, that no one would boast.
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them.
As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another, as good managers of the grace of God in its various forms.

lessons.still: When you sit down at work, look at your seat and say, “Lord, I did not grab this place; you prepared it. You have already set today’s good works before me. I only need to walk in them.”
teach: Paul first says, “By grace you have been saved through faith… not of works” (Ephesians 2:8–9). Only then does he add, “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10). The order matters: we are not saved by good works but saved for them. ‘Workmanship’ means a crafted piece — you are God’s handiwork, and the good works you will do he prepared in advance.

Walk into a wedding banquet and the place cards are already on the tables. You do not need to fight for a seat or worry that there is none, because the host has arranged it all. The good works God prepares are like that. Your gifts, personality and history, even your present role, are place cards God has set out. Peter says, “As each has received a gift, employ it in serving one another” (1 Peter 4:10). Staring at other tables only makes you miss the feast at your own.

The self-centred heart is always comparing: ‘Their gifts shine brighter; their role matters more.’ Comparison steals gratitude and drives us to use work to prove our worth. But your worth is already settled by grace. Good works are not chips to buy love; they are the response of someone already loved. When ‘I must prove myself’ becomes ‘I want to respond to grace’, you begin to shine right where you are.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of perspective — from ‘my performance decides my worth’ to ‘I am God’s workmanship’. The self-emptied life is not emptiness but entering the limitless in Christ: no need to compete, for God has prepared unique good works for each of us.
lessons.scene: Mei Ling is a senior associate at an accounting firm in Penang — careful and reliable, but not a natural presenter. When the department chooses someone to meet a new client, the manager picks a more articulate colleague. That evening at her small group, someone asks how she has been. She hesitates: should she say ‘Fine’, or share the hurt and the comparing in her heart?
q: Who is God? — God calls us “his workmanship”. What kind of craftsman is he?
Who am I? — Which part of yourself do you most often compare with others?
How shall I respond? — If you were Mei Ling, how might sharing honestly help her see the good works God has prepared?
lessons.jesus: Jesus never compared himself with anyone. He knew the path the Father had sent him on, so he could say, “I have accomplished the work which you have given me to do” (John 17:4). He did not do everything on earth, but he completed everything the Father gave him. In him, we need not do it all — only be faithful to the portion he sets before us.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for calling me your workmanship. I am saved entirely by grace, not by my performance. Heal my habit of comparing, so that I stop envying other people’s places and find faithful joy in the good works you have prepared. Today show me the one thing you have set before me, and make me willing to do it. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down three of your gifts and thank God for each
Sincerely praise a colleague you often compare yourself with
Ask the Lord: what good work have you prepared for me today?
lessons.noon: “We are his workmanship” — Lord, right now I stop comparing and stay faithful in the place you prepared.

lessons.title: Posted Where You Are
lessons.theme: You need not change places to serve; God calls you where you are

v: Only, as the Lord has distributed to each man, as God has called each, so let him walk. So I command in all the assemblies.
Was anyone called having been circumcised? Let him not become uncircumcised. Has anyone been called in uncircumcision? Let him not be circumcised.
Circumcision is nothing, and uncircumcision is nothing, but what matters is keeping God’s commandments.
Let each man stay in that calling in which he was called.
Brothers, let each man, in whatever condition he was called, stay in that condition with God.

lessons.still: Before you walk into the office, pause at the door or in the lift and pray, “Lord, I was called here, and here I serve you. Today I don’t ask for a different stage; I ask to be with you in this place.”
teach: After coming to faith, the Corinthians kept asking whether they needed a different status to be more spiritual. Paul says, “Let each man stay in that calling in which he was called” (1 Corinthians 7:20), and again, “stay in that condition with God” (1 Corinthians 7:24). The key is ‘with God’: not being trapped by circumstances, but being with God where you are. Paul is not forbidding change — “if you get an opportunity to become free, use it” (1 Corinthians 7:21). The point is that changing status is not a condition of being called.

When your company posts you to an overseas branch, you do not feel unimportant because you are away from head office. Quite the opposite: you know that because you are there, the company’s reach extends into that city. God has ‘posted’ you to that school, that hospital, that building site. You are not in the church office, but you are the kingdom’s local representative right there.

Some people feel that only ‘full-time ministry’ is the highest calling, so they drift through their present job. God does call some people to change direction, but a move should come from clear leading, not from escape. Letting Jesus be King means he decides where I am and what I do; my part is to hold this post faithfully today, before him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Humility is returning to our proper place. Holding the post God has assigned is letting God be God and people be people. Keep your focus on Jesus, not on circumstances; you can live an overcoming life anywhere.
lessons.scene: Junjie is a civil servant at a district office in Taipei and deeply involved in his church’s youth ministry. His pastor has invited him to join the staff full-time next year. He is thrilled, but he notices he has grown careless at work these past months, thinking, ‘I’m leaving anyway.’ Today his section chief asks him to take on a two-year project, and he does not know what to say.
q: Who is God? — Paul says to stay “with God”. How is God present with you in your role?
Who am I? — Have you ever treated your current job as merely a stopgap and stopped caring?
How shall I respond? — If you were Junjie, how could he answer his section chief honestly while seeking a full-time call?
lessons.jesus: At twelve, Jesus already knew, “I must be in my Father’s house” (Luke 2:49). Yet next “he went down with them and came to Nazareth. He was subject to them” (Luke 2:51), and stayed there for many years. He knew his calling clearly, yet he was in no hurry to leave his post; when the Father’s time came, he went to the cross without turning back.
lessons.pray: Lord, you called me in the place I am now. Forgive me for treating it as a stopgap and drifting. Help me hold my post before you, faithful, joyful and bright in this place. If you want to lead me onward, lead me clearly; until then, help me do every task in my hands well. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Finish one task you have been half-doing, properly, today
Pray one sentence each for your workplace and colleagues
If considering a move, arrange to talk with a mature believer
lessons.noon: “Stay in that condition with God” — Lord, right now I am with you in this place.

lessons.title: New Lenses for Monday
lessons.theme: Calling turns Monday from a chore into fresh mercy from God

v: It is because of The LORD’s loving kindnesses that we are not consumed, because his mercies don’t fail.
They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness.
Let the favour of the Lord our God be on us. Establish the work of our hands for us. Yes, establish the work of our hands.

lessons.still: When you wake on Monday, don’t reach for your phone. Sit on the edge of the bed and say, “Lord, your mercies are new every morning. Today I am not being dragged to work; I am being sent out by you.” Then get up.
teach: Lamentations was written among the ruins of a fallen city, yet the writer says, “They are new every morning. Great is your faithfulness” (Lamentations 3:23). His circumstances had not changed, but his sight had. In Psalm 90, Moses also prays, “Establish the work of our hands for us” (Psalm 90:17). Human work is fleeting, but God can establish it. Calling may not change what you do, but it changes the eyes with which you see it.

At the optician’s, you look at the chart while the optometrist swaps lens after lens: ‘Clearer like this, or like this?’ The chart stays the same, but with the right lens the blur becomes sharp. On Monday the office, the classroom or the ward is still the same place. But put on the lens of calling and you see that the difficult client is someone God loves, the repetitive report is a task God entrusted, and the commute is a road walked with the Lord.

This week we have learned that calling means coming to Jesus before being sent; that the Spirit fills the workshop; that God has prepared good works; and that we stay in our calling where we are. Change your thinking and your life changes; change your life and your daily living changes. Next Monday you need not wait to feel better before going out. You can step out with new sight, in the same place, and see God’s fresh mercy.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of perspective — from the temporary to the eternal, from the earthly to the heavenly. Change your thinking and your life changes; change your life and your living changes. Monday is still Monday, but I am wearing new lenses.
lessons.scene: Aroha teaches at a primary school in Auckland. Every Sunday evening her stomach knots and she cannot sleep, dreading Monday’s staff meeting and the parent who keeps complaining. Tonight she opens a job website again; on the desk beside her lies the ‘calling statement’ card from her small group.
q: Who is God? — Amid ruins the writer still said, “They are new every morning.” How dependable is God’s love?
Who am I? — Which ‘lenses’ do you usually wear on a Monday?
How shall I respond? — If you were Aroha, how could she prepare for tomorrow tonight with the eyes of calling?
lessons.jesus: Jesus rose “very early on the first day of the week” (Mark 16:2) — the first day of a new week. From that morning on, every week begins with resurrection hope. The Lord who conquered death can give a fresh start on your heaviest Monday too.
lessons.pray: Lord, your mercies are new every morning. Thank you for sending me out even on the Mondays I least want to go. Give me new eyes to see your purposes behind meetings, reports and clients. Establish the work of my hands, and make today’s labour meaningful in yours. I give you tomorrow’s meeting and all my worry. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: On Monday, read Lamentations 3:22–23 before checking your phone
Pray for the one person you most dread facing today
If anxiety or sleeplessness persists, talk to someone you trust
lessons.noon: “They are new every morning” — Lord, right now I look at this work with the new eyes you give.

mem.t: Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.

lessons.title: Even Instant Noodles for His Glory
lessons.theme: The most ordinary moments can become places that glorify God

v: Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.
Give no occasion for stumbling, whether to Jews, to Greeks, or to the assembly of God;
even as I also please all men in all things, not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many, that they may be saved.
Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ.
In that day there will be inscribed on the bells of the horses, “HOLY TO THE LORD”; and the pots in the LORD’s house will be like the bowls before the altar.

Yes, every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to the LORD of Armies; and all those who sacrifice will come and take of them, and cook in them. In that day there will no longer be a Canaanite in the house of the LORD of Armies.

lessons.still: As you eat breakfast or take your first sip of coffee, pause for thirty seconds and say, “Lord, even this mouthful comes from you. Today, whether I eat or drink, write or calculate, I want to do it all for your glory.”
teach: Paul is dealing with a very everyday dispute: may believers eat meat offered to idols? Yet his conclusion is enormous: “Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). He adds a direction: “not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many” (1 Corinthians 10:33). The prophet Zechariah saw a coming day when not only “the pots in the LORD’s house” but “every pot in Jerusalem and in Judah will be holy to the LORD of Armies” (Zechariah 14:20–21). A kitchen pot can be as holy as an altar bowl.

Official company documents often carry a watermark: a faint layer that never competes with the content, yet shows on every page whose document it is. ‘Do all to the glory of God’ is the watermark of a believer’s life. The emails you write, the accounts you balance, the meals you cook, the floors you mop look like ordinary work, but hold them up to the light and every page bears the Lord’s name.

The self-centred life cuts life into two pieces: the spiritual bit belongs to God, the everyday bit belongs to me. That is the sacred–secular divide. In 321 the focus is Jesus: not only Bible reading and prayer count; every small thing can be a place where Jesus is King. Queuing at the office kettle or listening to a colleague vent over lunch is a moment for him to receive glory.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The two cores — let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. ‘All’ includes lunchboxes, coffee and spreadsheets. Self-denial means living for Jesus and for others, not for myself: not seeking my own profit, but the profit of the many.
lessons.scene: Xiaoyun is a freelance illustrator who works from home, often eating instant noodles over a deadline. At lunchtime a client sends a third round of revisions in a curt tone. She puts down her chopsticks and types a sharp reply. Just as she is about to hit send, she notices the note stuck beside her screen: ‘Whatever you do, do all to the glory of God.’
q: Who is God? — If even kitchen pots can be ‘holy to the LORD’, in which corners of your life does God want to be honoured?
Who am I? — Which hours of your day feel as though they have ‘nothing to do with God’?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiaoyun, how would that note change the reply she sends?
lessons.jesus: Jesus often revealed the kingdom of God at the table: turning water into wine at a wedding in Cana, eating with tax collectors and sinners, breaking bread at the Last Supper, and after the resurrection cooking fish and bread over a charcoal fire for his disciples. He made the most ordinary meal a place where grace happens.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for today’s food and today’s work. Forgive me for splitting my life in two and thinking of you only on Sundays. Whether I eat or drink, write or calculate, let me do it all for your glory. When I want to fire off an angry message, remind me to seek not my own profit but the profit of the many. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before lunch, take ten seconds to give thanks for food and colleagues
Before sending an important message, ask: does this glorify God?
Do one small thing today for a colleague’s good
lessons.noon: “Whether therefore you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” — Lord, right now I offer even this lunch to you.

lessons.title: After the Veil Was Torn
lessons.theme: Jesus’ death opened a new way; we can come to God anywhere

v: Jesus cried again with a loud voice, and yielded up his spirit.
Behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom. The earth quaked and the rocks were split.
Having therefore, brothers, boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus,
by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh,

lessons.still: As you swipe into the building, think: this door needs a card, but the door to God Jesus has already opened for me. Say, “Lord, here too, today, I stand before you.”
teach: Jesus cried out with a loud voice and yielded up his spirit. “Behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom” (Matthew 27:51). That curtain separated the holy place from the most holy place, where only the high priest could enter, once a year. Torn from top to bottom — as if by God’s own hand. Hebrews explains that we have “boldness to enter into the holy place by the blood of Jesus, by the way which he dedicated for us, a new and living way, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh” (Hebrews 10:19–20).

Many companies divide their buildings with access cards: ordinary staff reach the open-plan office, managers can enter the server room, and the director’s suite needs special clearance. The Old Testament temple was zoned in much the same way. The cross upgrades your card to ‘all areas’ — not because of your rank, but because Jesus opened the door with his own body. From now on the ward, the building site and the kitchen can all be places where you come before God.

The sacred–secular divide makes us think God is present only at church or in quiet places. But the veil has already been torn. Change your thinking and your life changes: when you believe God is right there at your work, you can pray silently in a meeting, cry out under pressure and worship during overtime. This is not turning work into religious activity; it is letting every corner be filled with his presence.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Keep your focus on Jesus, not on circumstances. It is not the place that makes us holy; it is the way Jesus opened that lets us come to God at any moment. Relying on the Spirit, we can meet God anywhere.
lessons.scene: Jiahao is an emergency department nurse at a hospital in Kaohsiung. His shift pattern has kept him from church for six Sundays in a row. His small-group leader messages to check in, and Jiahao does not know how to reply; he feels further and further from God. At three this morning a patient’s relative breaks down sobbing in the corridor. Standing at the nurses’ station, Jiahao hesitates over whether to sit with her and say a short prayer.
q: Who is God? — The veil was torn from top to bottom. How much does God long to draw near to us?
Who am I? — Do you also feel you are only ‘before God’ at church or in quiet moments?
How shall I respond? — If you were Jiahao, how could he experience, and carry, God’s presence in the emergency department at 3 a.m.?
lessons.jesus: The veil was torn because Jesus’ body was torn first. On the cross he bore separation from the Father so that we would never again be shut out. This High Priest does not stand behind the curtain passing on messages; he himself has become the new and living way.
lessons.pray: Lord Jesus, thank you for opening a new and living way through your own body. Forgive me for thinking you are found only in church. Today at my desk, on the ward, on the site or in the kitchen, let me know that I stand before you. In hectic moments remind me I can call on you at once; on weary night shifts, let me know you are near. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Choose one spot at work as your quiet ‘prayer corner’
Before a meeting or a rush, call on the Lord in one sentence
If work has kept you from church, contact a fellow believer
lessons.noon: “The veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom” — Lord, right now, right here, I come boldly before you.

lessons.title: Five, Two and One
lessons.theme: The Lord entrusts his goods to servants in every line of work

v: “For it is like a man going into another country, who called his own servants and entrusted his goods to them.
To one he gave five talents, to another two, to another one, to each according to his own ability. Then he went on his journey.
Immediately he who received the five talents went and traded with them, and made another five talents.
In the same way, he also who got the two gained another two.
But he who received the one talent went away and dug in the earth and hid his lord’s money.
“Now after a long time the lord of those servants came, and settled accounts with them.
He who received the five talents came and brought another five talents, saying, ‘Lord, you delivered to me five talents. Behold, I have gained another five talents in addition to them.’
“His lord said to him, ‘Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things, I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of your lord.’

lessons.still: As you open today’s calendar, say, “Lord, this time, these abilities and these resources are goods you have entrusted to me. Today I won’t bury them; I will put them to work for you.” Then circle the most important task.
teach: A man about to travel abroad “called his own servants and entrusted his goods to them”, giving “to each according to his own ability” (Matthew 25:14–15). Not everyone received the same amount, but everyone received something. Two servants “immediately” went and traded; the third “dug in the earth” and hid his master’s money. When the master returned to settle accounts, he did not praise the size of the profit but the character of the servant: “Well done, good and faithful servant. You have been faithful over a few things” (Matthew 25:21).

Picture a chain of shops opening branches everywhere: one in a shopping centre, one at a night market, one beside a small-town station. Head office gives each branch a different size, but every manager receives the same operations manual and hangs the same sign. God’s kingdom is like that. Some serve in banks, some at noodle stalls, some in classrooms, some at home caring for children. Each place is one of his branches, and you are its manager.

The servant who buried his talent said, “I was afraid” (Matthew 25:25). Fear and comparison tell us, ‘My post is too small to bother with.’ But in God’s kingdom there are no small posts, only faithful or unfaithful servants. Letting Jesus be King means trusting that what he has given me is exactly right, and bravely putting it to work so that it bears fruit for him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Building God’s order — the kingdom’s servants are scattered across every trade, and each place is his household. Change your thinking from ‘my work doesn’t matter’ to ‘this is what the Lord has entrusted to me’.
lessons.scene: Shufen has sold vegetables at a market in Tainan for twenty years. Her church is holding a ‘workplace testimony’ evening and asks everyone to write down what their work means. Looking at the list — doctors, lawyers, engineers — she feels she is ‘just a vegetable seller’ and wants to screw up the form. Just then the elderly stallholder next door leans over: ‘Why do you always give customers a few extra spring onions, and remember all their names?’
q: Who is God? — The master entrusted goods according to each one’s ability. What does this say about how God sees each person?
Who am I? — Have you ever felt you were given ‘only one talent’? How did you respond?
How shall I respond? — If you were Shufen, how might her neighbour’s question change the way she sees her work?
lessons.jesus: Jesus himself is the most faithful servant. He said, “The Son of Man also came not to be served but to serve” (Mark 10:45). He put everything the Father entrusted to him to work, even to giving his life. Because of his faithfulness, fearful servants like us may still hear the master say, “Enter into the joy of your lord.”
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for entrusting your goods to me; whether much or little, it is a sign of your trust. Forgive me for burying my gifts out of fear or comparison. Today at my stall, counter or desk, make me bold to put to work all you have given me. I don’t ask to be big, only to be faithful in a few things, so that people see you through me. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down three ‘talents’ you hold: time, skills, contacts
Put one buried ability to use today
Pray one sentence for other believers in your industry
lessons.noon: “You have been faithful over a few things” — Lord, right now I want to be faithful to you in this small thing.

lessons.title: Sunday Worship’s Extension Lead
lessons.theme: Worship does not end on Sunday; it extends into every workday

v: Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service.
Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.

lessons.still: As you sit down at your desk, sing a line from last Sunday’s worship quietly in your heart. Say, “Lord, Sunday’s worship isn’t over. Today, here, I carry on worshipping you.”
teach: After eleven chapters on God’s great salvation, Paul opens Romans 12 with, “Therefore I urge you, brothers, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service” (Romans 12:1). The word for ‘service’ also carries the sense of worship. The worship Paul wants is not only in the temple; it is the offering of the body — your hands, feet, eyes and hours, the very you who goes to work from Monday to Friday.

There is only one socket on the wall, but you can plug in an extension lead and carry power to the desk, the kitchen or the balcony. Sunday worship is like that socket: there we meet God and are filled. But God wants us to run an extension lead, carrying that worship to the desk, the counter and the classroom. If there is power only next to the socket, the other six days of life go dark.

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). The world’s workplace says, ‘Winner takes all; look after yourself first.’ A renewed mind says, ‘Let Jesus be King.’ This is the step of practice among the eight steps: the information and revelation received on Sunday must be lived out on Monday. A renewed mind brings a transformed life, so that people can prove through your work what is the good, well-pleasing and perfect will of God.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The fivefold change from the inside out — first thinking, then life, flowing into daily living, relationships and ministry. Worship begins with a renewed mind, but it must be visible at work.
lessons.scene: Pastor Huang leads a church in New Taipei, and Monday is his admin day. This morning his inbox holds forty unread emails: venue bookings, financial reports and a letter of complaint from a church member. Only yesterday he preached that ‘Sunday worship should extend to the office desk’, yet right now he is irritable enough to shut the laptop and go for a coffee first.
q: Who is God? — Paul appeals to us “by the mercies of God”. Where do you see traces of his mercy in your life?
Who am I? — After Sunday worship, on which day and at what moment does your ‘power’ usually cut out?
How shall I respond? — If you were Pastor Huang, facing forty emails and a complaint, how could he let worship extend into the morning?
lessons.jesus: Jesus’ worship was never confined to the synagogue. By a well he told a Samaritan woman, “The true worshippers will worship the Father in spirit and truth” (John 4:23). He himself is the perfect living sacrifice, offering his whole self to the Father; because of him, our bodies too can become a sacrifice that pleases God.
lessons.pray: Lord, thank you for your mercy, which lets me present my body as a living sacrifice. Forgive me for leaving worship on Sunday and losing power as soon as Monday comes. In every email and every meeting today, renew my mind, so that I am not conformed to the world’s anxiety and point-scoring. Let my work be worship that carries on. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: On the way to work, listen to a song from Sunday’s service
Before your most irritating task, say: ‘Lord, this too is worship’
Write down one line from Sunday’s sermon and practise it today
lessons.noon: “Present your bodies a living sacrifice” — Lord, right now this desk is my altar.

lessons.title: Ask the Lord to Sign for Today
lessons.theme: Every piece of work can become a spiritual sacrifice to God

v: Come to him, a living stone, rejected indeed by men, but chosen by God, precious.
You also as living stones are built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ.
Through him, then, let’s offer up a sacrifice of praise to God continually, that is, the fruit of lips which proclaim allegiance to his name.
But don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased.

lessons.still: Before you leave work, or as you finish a task, close your eyes for thirty seconds, fold your hands and say, “Lord, what I finished and what I didn’t, what went well and what didn’t, I place in your hands. Please accept it.”
teach: In the Old Testament, priests offered sacrifices in the temple; in the New Testament, believers themselves are priests. Peter says we are “living stones… built up as a spiritual house, to be a holy priesthood, to offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 2:5). Hebrews tells us what such sacrifices include: “a sacrifice of praise to God continually”, and “don’t forget to be doing good and sharing, for with such sacrifices God is well pleased” (Hebrews 13:15–16). Praise on the lips and good deeds in the hands are both offerings.

When a delivery rider brings food to your door, the last step is asking you to sign for it. Without the signature, the order is not complete. Our work needs a moment of signing too: at the end of each day, place your results, your mistakes and your sweat in the Lord’s hands and ask him to sign for them. What is good, he accepts; what is not, he forgives and corrects. The point is not doing it perfectly, but offering it ‘through Jesus Christ’ — he is the one who makes our sacrifice acceptable.

This week we have broken down the sacred–secular divide: whether we eat or drink, all is for God’s glory; the veil is torn, and every place is holy ground; every trade is part of God’s household; Sunday worship extends to the office desk. The self-centred person treats work as their own masterpiece, demanding a signature and applause. The self-emptied person treats work as an offering to God and lets Jesus receive all the glory. Today, offer your work to him.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The self-emptied life — it is no longer I, but Christ who lives in me. Offering work as a living sacrifice is self-denial: for Jesus, for others, not for myself. Let Jesus receive all the glory, even the applause.
lessons.scene: Xiaodong works in sales for a software company in Shanghai. Before quarter-end he stayed up all night producing a brilliant proposal; at the next day’s meeting, his manager presented it as his own work. Afterwards colleagues urge him to email the director ‘to set the record straight’. Xiaodong sits back down and opens a draft email, the cursor blinking.
q: Who is God? — God accepts spiritual sacrifices offered “through Jesus Christ”. How does this change the way you view your imperfect work?
Who am I? — Whose signature do you most crave on your work?
How shall I respond? — If you were Xiaodong, how would offering his work to God shape what he does with that draft: send it, delete it, or speak another way?
lessons.jesus: On the cross Jesus offered the most perfect sacrifice. He was misunderstood and rejected; “when he was cursed, he didn’t curse back”, but committed himself to him who judges righteously (1 Peter 2:23). Because of his offering, even our imperfect work is made acceptable to God through him.
lessons.pray: Lord, I offer you today’s work: what is finished and unfinished, what was noticed and what was taken from me — all of it is in your hands. Thank you for accepting my spiritual sacrifice through Jesus. Heal my hunger for applause; let me offer praise as a sacrifice and not forget to do good. When I meet unfairness, give me wisdom and gentleness. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Before leaving, take one minute to have the Lord ‘sign for’ today
Offer God one sentence of praise for something today
Do one unrewarded kindness, like helping a colleague finish up
lessons.noon: “To offer up spiritual sacrifices, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ” — Lord, right now I offer you the work in my hands.

mem.t: Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lords work, because you know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

lessons.title: Work Among the Thorns
lessons.theme: Toil is not the true nature of work but the damage sin has done

v: To Adam he said, “Because you have listened to your wife’s voice, and have eaten from the tree, about which I commanded you, saying, ‘You shall not eat of it,’ the ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labour all the days of your life.
It will yield thorns and thistles to you; and you will eat the herb of the field.
You will eat bread by the sweat of your face until you return to the ground, for you were taken out of it. For you are dust, and you shall return to dust.”
For the creation was subjected to vanity, not of its own will, but because of him who subjected it, in hope
that the creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of decay into the liberty of the glory of the children of God.

lessons.still: Before you tackle the task you least want to do today, pause for thirty seconds and say honestly, “Lord, this wears me out and frustrates me. I won’t pretend to like it, but I give this toil to you. Please be with me in it.”
teach: God said to Adam, “The ground is cursed for your sake. You will eat from it with much labour all the days of your life” (Genesis 3:17). Notice that what is cursed is the ground, not work itself. Work existed before the fall; after the fall came “thorns and thistles” and bread eaten “by the sweat of your face” (Genesis 3:18–19). Paul says “the creation was subjected to vanity”, yet waits in hope to “be delivered from the bondage of decay” (Romans 8:20–21). Today’s frustrations at work — wasted effort, unfairness, setbacks — are the marks of that damage.

When a computer catches a virus, it does not mean the computer was badly made. It was well designed, but once infected it starts crashing, slowing down and throwing up strange error messages. Work is like that. God’s original design was good, but sin got in like a virus, and now our labour keeps freezing: projects stall, colleagues clash, effort disappears into the system. Seeing this, we stop blaming work itself for everything, and stop naively thinking a new job will have no thorns.

The root of toil is our wanting to be in charge, leaving our place as creatures. That is where the self-centred life begins: Adam did not want God as King, and even the ground turned against him. The good news is that there is a cure for the virus. Redemption does not mean escaping work; it means letting Jesus be King again, bringing our toil back, bit by bit, to God’s original purpose. The sweat you shed today will not be wasted in his hands.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Self-centredness is the root of the fall — we wanted to replace God as King, and toil followed. Pride is leaving our place to seize power. Returning to our place and letting God be God is where the healing of toil begins.
lessons.scene: Meihui is a full-time mum with three children and a father-in-law who needs daily care. Laundry, cooking, school runs, medicines — the work often runs late into the night. Tonight she has just mopped the floor when her youngest knocks over a glass of juice. Standing in the kitchen with the mop in her hand and tears close, she does not know whether to shout at him or take a deep breath first.
q: Who is God? — Even under the curse, God still let people eat from the ground. What kindness does this show?
Who am I? — Which kind of ‘thorn’ in your work most often makes you want to give up?
How shall I respond? — If you were Meihui, how could she hand her toil to the Lord in that moment, rather than taking it out on her child?
lessons.jesus: The soldiers “braided a crown of thorns and put it on his head” (Matthew 27:29). Thorns were the sign of the curse, and Jesus wore them himself. In Gethsemane, as he prayed, “his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down on the ground” (Luke 22:44). He bore the thorns and the sweat so that our toil could be redeemed.
lessons.pray: Lord, I admit that today’s work has many thorns, and I am often tired. Thank you for wearing the crown of thorns and bearing my curse. Be with me when the sweat runs down my face, and keep me from taking my anger out on others. Bring my toil back to your first good purpose, and make it meaningful in your hands. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Tell the Lord honestly about one task that drains you
When you hit a ‘thorn’, take three deep breaths before responding
If you are running on empty, ask family or someone you trust for help
lessons.noon: “The creation itself also will be delivered from the bondage of decay” — Lord, right now, in this hard work, I still look to your redemption.

lessons.title: Babel’s Neon Sign
lessons.theme: Work done to make a name for ourselves will one day stop

v: The whole earth was of one language and of one speech.
As they travelled east, they found a plain in the land of Shinar, and they lived there.
They said to one another, “Come, let’s make bricks, and burn them thoroughly.” They had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar.
They said, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth.”
The LORD came down to see the city and the tower, which the children of men built.
The LORD said, “Behold, they are one people, and they all have one language, and this is what they begin to do. Now nothing will be withheld from them, which they intend to do.
Come, let’s go down, and there confuse their language, that they may not understand one another’s speech.”
So the LORD scattered them abroad from there on the surface of all the earth. They stopped building the city.
Therefore its name was called Babel, because there the LORD confused the language of all the earth. From there, the LORD scattered them abroad on the surface of all the earth.

lessons.still: As you log in, glance at your name or username on the screen and say, “Lord, today I am not making a name for myself. May your name be lifted high; my name is safe enough in your hands.”
teach: After the flood, people on the plain of Shinar said to one another, “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth” (Genesis 11:4). Their technology had advanced — “they had brick for stone, and they used tar for mortar” (Genesis 11:3). The problem was not building a tower but the motive: making a name for themselves and resisting God’s purpose that they should fill the earth. So “the LORD came down to see the city and the tower”, confused their language, and “they stopped building the city” (Genesis 11:5, 8).

At night the brightest thing in a city skyline is often the neon sign on top of a tower. Companies spend fortunes making their names huge and dazzling so the whole street can see. Yet the bigger the sign, the easier it is to forget that a building exists to serve people, not to display a name. Much of our striving at work quietly becomes a Babel — CV, job title, personal brand, stacked layer upon layer, all to make a name for ourselves.

The deepest expression of self-centredness is wanting to replace God and make a name for ourselves. At Babel God stopped the building in order to halt pride before it ran its full course. In the very next chapter, God freely promises Abram, “I will… make your name great” (Genesis 12:2). A name is not something we seize but something God gives. Humility is the key to revival: when we stop making a name for ourselves, God in his time makes our work a channel of blessing to the nations.
lessons.light: 321 Light: Pride is leaving our place to seize power; the builders of Babel tried to seize heaven. Humility is laying down power and returning to our place. Letting Jesus receive all the glory means replacing the name on the sign with his.
lessons.scene: Darren is the founder of a start-up in Singapore that has just closed a funding round. Before a media interview, his PR adviser suggests he describe the whole team’s achievement as ‘something I built single-handedly’, because ‘investors love a hero story’. Darren looks at the question on the brief — ‘What is the secret of your success?’ — his pen hovering in mid-air.
q: Who is God? — God came down to see Babel and then stopped the building. Was that judgement, or protection?
Who am I? — Is any part of your work quietly becoming a way to make a name for yourself?
How shall I respond? — If you were Darren, how could he answer ‘the secret of your success’ honestly, without belittling himself?
lessons.jesus: Jesus is the only one truly worthy of a great name, yet he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7). He did not make a name for himself; instead “God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9). In him we see that the way up is the way down.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often want to make a name for myself — on my CV, in meetings, on social media. Tear down the Babel in my heart, so that I no longer find my security in my own name. May your name be lifted high in my work. I place my name in your hands; make my work a channel of blessing to others. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: In a report or meeting, name one colleague’s specific contribution
Look at your social media bio and ask: who does this exalt?
Sincerely bless a competitor’s success
lessons.noon: “Let’s make a name for ourselves” — Lord, right now I let go of making my own name; may your name be lifted high.

lessons.title: The Treadmill Under the Sun
lessons.theme: Labour without God is vanity; received from his hand, it has meaning

v: Therefore I began to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labour in which I had laboured under the sun.
For there is a man whose labour is with wisdom, with knowledge, and with skilfulness; yet he shall leave it for his portion to a man who has not laboured for it. This also is vanity and a great evil.
For what does a man have of all his labour and of the striving of his heart, in which he labours under the sun?
For all his days are sorrows, and his travail is grief; yes, even in the night his heart takes no rest. This also is vanity.
There is nothing better for a man than that he should eat and drink, and make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God.
He has made everything beautiful in its time. He has also set eternity in their hearts, yet so that man can’t find out the work that God has done from the beginning even to the end.

lessons.still: Before work, look out of the window at the sky and pause for thirty seconds. Say, “Lord, I don’t want to go round in circles under the sun. Let me receive today’s labour from your hand, and give it back into your hand.”
teach: The Preacher had everything: wealth, wisdom, great building projects. Yet he says, “I began to cause my heart to despair concerning all the labour in which I had laboured under the sun” (Ecclesiastes 2:20). “What does a man have of all his labour and of the striving of his heart, in which he labours under the sun?” (Ecclesiastes 2:22). ‘Under the sun’ is the key phrase of Ecclesiastes: life seen only from an earthly viewpoint, leaving God out of the reckoning. There, even the most successful work is ‘vanity’ — a breath, a puff of smoke.

The gym treadmill is honest: you run until you are drenched in sweat, your heart rate soars and the distance keeps climbing — yet when you look up, you are exactly where you started. Work under the sun is often like a treadmill. KPIs reset every year, sales go back to zero every quarter, and every promotion is followed by the next target. However fast you run, if your direction is only earthly, you end up where you began. “This also is vanity.”

But Ecclesiastes does not only speak of vanity. The Preacher also sees that to “make his soul enjoy good in his labour… is from the hand of God” (Ecclesiastes 2:24), and that God “has also set eternity in their hearts” (Ecclesiastes 3:11). A change of perspective — from under the sun to above it, from the temporary to the eternal. When work is received from God’s hand, the treadmill becomes a road. The work has not changed; what has changed is that you know where it leads.
lessons.light: 321 Light: A change of perspective — earthly to heavenly, temporary to eternal. Focus on Jesus, not on targets. Rely on the heart and you find joy; rely on the head and you find worry: calculating our labour apart from God turns toil into the grief the Preacher describes.
lessons.scene: Zhang Huimin worked in finance at a multinational for twenty-two years, until she was made redundant at fifty-three. She once believed she was indispensable; now she wakes each morning unsure whether to put on work clothes or stay in her pyjamas. Today a small charity has invited her to be their part-time accountant, on a third of her former salary. She looks at the letter and still has not replied.
q: Who is God? — God “has also set eternity in their hearts”. Why won’t he let us be satisfied with life under the sun alone?
Who am I? — Which parts of your work feel like running on a treadmill?
How shall I respond? — If you were Huimin, how could she think about that part-time offer from a viewpoint ‘above the sun’?
lessons.jesus: The Preacher found no answer under the sun, but Jesus came from above the sun to live under it. He said, “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly” (John 10:10). In him, labour is no longer a puff of smoke but a path into eternal abundance.
lessons.pray: Lord, I confess that I often run under the sun, chasing the next target while my heart feels empty. Thank you for setting eternity in my heart, so that I know only you can satisfy. Change my perspective, so that I receive my work from your hand and find good even in my labour. If I am standing at a crossroads of loss or change, lead me yourself. In the name of the Lord Jesus, Amen.
acts: Write down a goal you keep chasing that never satisfies
Thank God today for one small result of your work
If facing job loss, ask a spiritual companion to pray with you
lessons.noon: “Make his soul enjoy good in his labour. This also I saw, that it is from the hand of God” — Lord, right now I receive this work from your hand.

lessons.title: Resurrection Cloud Backup
lessons.theme: Because of the resurrection, labour in the Lord is not in vain

v: But when this perishable body will have become imperishable, and this mortal will have put on immortality, then what is written will happen: “Death is swallowed up in victory.”
“Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory?”
The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law.
But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore, my beloved brothers, be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord.

lessons.still: The first time you save a file today, pause and say, “Lord, you said that labour in you is not in vain. You remember everything I do today.” Then press save.
teach: 1 Corinthians 15 is the fullest chapter on the resurrection in the Bible. Paul declares, “Death is swallowed up in victory… thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:54, 57). The ‘therefore’ that follows is not about heaven but about work: “Be steadfast, immovable, always abounding in the Lord’s work, because you know that your labour is not in vain in the Lord” (1 Corinthians 15:58). Resurrection hope lands right in the workplace as motivation.

We all remember the despair of a computer crash wiping out an unsaved report. Today many of us use automatic cloud backup: even if the laptop dies, the files are safe somewhere else. The resurrection is like God’s cloud. What we do in the Lord is not wiped clean when a project is cancelled, a company folds, or even when we die. God sees, God remembers, and he will reveal it on that day.

This does not mean every piece of work will be preserved exactly as it is, but that faithfulness, love and goodness in the Lord have eternal worth. The self-centred person stakes the meaning of labour on results: success makes it worthwhile, failure makes it wasted. The self-emptied person hands their labour to the Lord: the results are in his hands, faithfulness is in mine. This is the overcomer’s outlook — not because work always goes well, but because the Lord has already conquered death.
lessons.light: 321 Light: The goal is to become an overcomer who will one day sit with Christ on his throne and reign with him. Labour in the Lord is not in vain — a shift from the temporary to the eternal, with our focus on the risen Lord rather than on passing success or failure.
lessons.scene: Tane is a site foreman in Hamilton, New Zealand. He has led his crew for eighteen months building a community centre. Just before completion, the developer announces that the project is suspended for lack of funds and may never open. The crew are downcast; someone says, ‘That was eighteen months for nothing.’ Tane stands in the middle of the empty site, and everyone waits for him to speak.
q: Who is God? — The risen Lord declares that death is swallowed up. How does he see your seemingly wasted effort?
Who am I? — Has any recent piece of work left you feeling it was ‘all for nothing’?
How shall I respond? — If you were Tane, what could he say to that discouraged crew?
lessons.jesus: At the foot of the cross, Jesus’ three years of work looked completely wasted: the disciples scattered, their Lord crucified, the tomb sealed. But on the third day he rose. The moment that looked most in vain was God’s greatest work. The risen Lord guarantees that nothing placed in his hands is ever wasted.
